pages.title: Home
About Us
pages.content:
Since 2011, from Collingwood

Yanagi Hygiene was founded in 2011 by Hana Yanagi to bring clinical infection-control discipline to commercial pest management across Melbourne. Based at 41 Wellington Street in Collingwood, our team of fourteen works within sixty kilometres of our depot.

Why did a hospital infection-control officer establish a commercial pest firm?

In 2011, Hana Yanagi left her role as a hospital infection-control officer to establish Yanagi Hygiene in Collingwood. In hospital wards, preventing contamination relies on rigorous environmental inspection, understanding entry pathways, and identifying structural vulnerabilities long before outbreaks occur. Hana recognised that commercial kitchens, hotels, and warehouses were too often treated with routine chemical spraying rather than careful physical investigation. Instead of masking symptoms, our practice prioritises finding where pests enter, feed, and harbour. We inspect the unmonitored voids, drains, and risers where problems actually originate, applying clinical hygiene standards to commercial properties across Melbourne.

Why do we always conduct an inspection hour before proposing a plan?

Every building has unique vulnerabilities that cannot be understood from an office desk or estimated from square metres alone. During our sixty-minute initial inspection, we walk the site directly with the facilities manager, looking where others rarely look. We examine ceiling voids, sub-floor areas, pipe penetrations, and loading dock seals. Within that single hour, up to one thousand square metres are mapped and physically assessed. We leave a handwritten findings sheet on site at the sixtieth minute, ensuring complete transparency before recommending a four, six, or twelve-visit seasonal plan tailored to the building's genuine physical condition.

Why are written records kept for three years beyond the plan term?

Accountability in hygiene management requires an unbroken paper trail. Priya Nair leads our documentation, drafting findings sheet templates that capture every numbered monitor station and structural breach. A signed findings sheet is left on site immediately following each visit, followed by a formal written report emailed within two working days. We retain these comprehensive site logs for the entire life of your service plan plus an additional three years. This permanent record provides facility managers, auditors, and health authorities with verifiable proof of ongoing structural maintenance, monitoring observations, and corrective physical actions.

Who are the team members responsible for your site?

Our Collingwood depot employs fourteen dedicated specialists. Hana Yanagi leads field operations and conducts initial inspection hours. Senior technician Tomás Ferreira oversees kitchens and food production facilities. Amara Mensah manages hotels and complex mixed-use buildings, while Liam O'Connell inspects warehouses, loading docks, and cold storage facilities. Priya Nair directs our reporting standards and findings documentation. Jonas Weber, our staff entomologist, leads ongoing technical training and species identification. At the desk, Grace Tan coordinates scheduling, booking inspection hours and managing routine visit calendars for every commercial client.

pages.title: Sites We Look After
pages.content:
Six places we look first

We manage commercial environments within sixty kilometres of our Collingwood depot, focusing on structural boundaries and hidden service cavities. Our seasonal routines are tailored specifically to the operational rhythms of each building type.

How do we inspect commercial kitchens and food production facilities?

Commercial food lines demand relentless scrutiny of heat and moisture sources. We inspect beneath heavy cooking equipment, behind refrigeration seals, and inside low floor drains where organic matter collects. In a Fitzroy corner restaurant with sixty seats and an overhead office floor, our initial inspection revealed an unsealed dishwasher drain gap and an open cable riser extending directly into the ceiling void, leading to a dedicated six-visit plan. Senior technician Tomás Ferreira maps every monitoring point to ensure food handling areas remain undisturbed during critical prep hours.

What makes loading docks and cold stores vulnerable to entry?

Loading docks represent the primary physical gateway between outdoor environments and commercial stock. Technicians examine overhead roller door tracks, dock leveler pits, and rubber perimeter seals for daylight gaps. At a two thousand four hundred square metre cold-store warehouse in Port Melbourne with four dock doors, our inspection identified degraded dock perimeter seals and uncontained pallet-wrap waste, establishing a six-visit plan with dock seals inspected first. Liam O'Connell inspects door brush strips, dock cushions, and surrounding staging zones on every scheduled seasonal round.

How are office floors and shared kitchenettes maintained across the year?

Multi-level office buildings contain expansive horizontal cable trays and vertical service risers that connect separate tenancies. In a three-storey office building in Richmond with a shared ground bin store, persistent waste issues in common kitchenettes determined a balanced four-visit annual plan. We examine false ceiling tiles, electrical conduits, plumbing chases, and under-sink cabinetry across all tenant floors. Scheduled visits are booked between 05:30 and 23:00 to ensure thorough investigation takes place without interrupting office workers or corporate meetings.

Why do bin stores, ceiling voids, and plant rooms require dedicated focus?

Waste rooms and mechanical spaces sustain pest populations if neglected. In basement bin stores, we inspect floor waste drains, perimeter brickwork, and bin lid integrity. Inside suspended ceiling voids, we trace cable pathways and ducting connections where rodents travel undetected. Rooftop plant rooms and condenser housings are checked for external bird netting gaps and weather seal degradation. By systematically opening these six core areas—kitchen lines, loading docks, office floors, bin stores, ceiling voids, and plant rooms—we eliminate unmonitored harbourage zones.

pages.title: The Inspection Hour
pages.content:
Sixty minutes, written down on site

The inspection hour is a sixty-minute on-site investigation of up to one thousand square metres, priced at AUD 180 including GST. The fee is credited in full to your first annual plan if started within thirty days.

00–10 min · Walk the floor plan

Walk the floor plan with the facilities manager: where deliveries arrive, where food and waste sit, what has been seen.

10–35 min · Look where nobody looks

Ceiling voids, under kitchen lines, drains, risers, dock seals, plant rooms.

35–50 min · Map the points

Monitors and stations marked on your floor plan, each with a number.

50–60 min · Write it down on site

A one-page findings sheet signed by both of you, with the plan we would suggest.

00–35 min

How are the first thirty-five minutes of the hour structured?

The inspection begins with ten minutes walking the site alongside the facilities manager. We review floor plans, identify delivery bays, inspect waste storage locations, and discuss previous pest sightings. From minute ten to minute thirty-five, our technician investigates where nobody looks. Equipped with a high-powered inspection torch, telescopic mirror, and precision gap gauge, we examine ceiling voids, sub-floor cavities, pipe penetrations, refrigeration motors, loading dock seals, and mechanical plant rooms. We identify hidden structural gaps and moisture traps before pest activity spreads into active work areas.

35–60 min

What occurs during the final twenty-five minutes on site?

From minute thirty-five to minute fifty, we map the facility. Every critical vulnerability, monitor station, and mechanical trap is marked directly on your site floor plan with a unique reference number. Between minute fifty and minute sixty, we complete a concise one-page findings sheet on site. The technician notes immediate structural faults, hygiene recommendations, and our suggested seasonal visit plan. Both the technician and facilities manager sign the document before we leave, providing immediate written documentation prior to the formal report emailed within two working days.

What is in the case

Torch

A narrow, bright beam for voids, risers and under kitchen lines.

Inspection mirror

Reaches behind motors and under plant where a head cannot.

Gap gauge

Every gap on the sheet is measured in millimetres, not guessed.

Monitor station

Numbered, placed out of the way of trade and marked on your plan.

Moisture meter

Finds the damp that draws pests before they arrive.

What should your facility team prepare prior to our arrival?

To maximise the sixty-minute inspection, facilities managers should have an accurate printed floor plan ready upon arrival. Please ensure keys, access fobs, and padlock codes for locked plant rooms, roof hatches, electrical risers, and waste compounds are accessible. A staff member familiar with daily deliveries, waste disposal routines, and tenant reports must accompany our technician throughout the hour. Inspections are booked between 05:30 and 23:00, allowing investigations to take place before opening, during shift transitions, or after evening trade without interrupting daily commercial operations.

pages.title: The Treatment Year
pages.content:
Four visits a year, one per season

Our annual service agreements provide structured seasonal maintenance across twelve months with four scheduled visits. Agreements require thirty days of notice from either party to conclude.

February

Late summer: loading docks, outside waste areas and the hottest kitchen equipment.

May

Autumn: plant rooms, ceiling voids and cable risers as the weather turns.

August

Winter: moisture traps, sub-floor vents and the edges of the building.

November

Spring: dock door sweeps, monitor stations, outside bin areas and window screens.

What seasonal tasks are completed across the four quarterly visits?

Our standard annual agreement covers four visits aligned with Melbourne's seasonal shifts: February, May, August, and November. In February, late-summer inspections concentrate on loading docks, external waste zones, and high-temperature kitchen equipment. In May, our technicians inspect warm plant rooms, ceiling voids, and cable risers for rodent sheltering as autumn temperatures decline. In August, winter assessments focus on internal moisture traps, sub-floor vents, and perimeter foundations. In November, spring servicing prioritises dock door sweeps, insect monitoring stations, external bin areas, and window screening ahead of summer activity.

What are our annual plan tiers and transparent service fees?

All service fees are quoted in Australian dollars, including GST. An initial inspection hour of up to one thousand square metres costs AUD 180, credited if a plan begins within thirty days. Small kitchens and cafés up to two hundred and fifty square metres receive four annual visits for AUD 1,480. Restaurants and food production facilities between two hundred and fifty and eight hundred square metres receive six visits for AUD 2,640. Office buildings up to three floors of one thousand square metres cost AUD 1,960 for four visits. Warehouses up to three thousand square metres cost AUD 3,420 for six visits. Hotel and mixed-use properties receive twelve visits from AUD 6,900. Call-outs between scheduled visits are AUD 220, included at no extra charge on twelve-visit plans.

How do our twelve-month agreement terms operate?

Every service agreement runs for a twelve-month period and operates without lock-in penalties. Either party may terminate the agreement at any point by providing thirty days written notice. We do not offer unrealistic promises of a pest-free environment; instead, our commitment is visits, looking, records, and a plan. We provide rigorous physical inspections, uncompromised record-keeping, scheduled preventive visits, and practical building remediation advice. Visits are booked from 05:30 to 23:00 on any day of the week, allowing service to occur around your commercial trading hours across Melbourne.

pages.title: Records and Compliance
pages.content:
Signed sheets, kept for the life of the plan plus 3 years

Verifiable records protect commercial facilities during environmental health inspections and compliance audits. Every Yanagi Hygiene visit concludes with a signed physical findings sheet left on site.

01 · Back door sweep

A 6 mm gap under the back door sweep, noted with its number on your plan.

04 · Dishwasher drain

The drain and the wall behind it, checked every visit.

07 · Dock seal gap 9 mm

Measured with the gap gauge, daylight visible, repair on the list.

09 · Dry store shelf

Shelf backs and the floor under them, torch and mirror.

12 · Bin store lid

Lid seal and washdown point, with what your team can change.

What specific information is documented on the site findings sheet?

Priya Nair oversees our reporting standards to ensure every site document meets strict regulatory benchmarks. At the conclusion of every visit, we leave a one-page findings sheet signed by our technician and your facility representative. This document references a numbered site floor plan showing precise monitoring locations—such as Point 01 for a back door sweep gap of six millimetres, Point 04 at a dishwasher drain, Point 07 indicating a dock seal gap of nine millimetres, Point 09 inside a dry store shelf, or Point 12 on a bin store lid. It records what we found, physical adjustments made, required client maintenance, and the scheduled date for your next seasonal visit.

How long are inspection records maintained in our permanent archive?

A comprehensive digital inspection report is delivered via email within two working days of every completed visit. Yanagi Hygiene securely archives every floor plan, findings sheet, and technician log for the entire duration of your twelve-month plan plus an additional three years. This permanent archive ensures your business maintains an unbroken compliance record for municipal health authorities, internal quality auditors, and commercial insurers. Whether your site requires historical documentation for a past tenancy or verification of past structural repairs, our Collingwood desk retrieves signed records upon request.

How did structured records assist a Southbank hotel facility?

In a high-density Southbank hotel containing one hundred and eighteen rooms across multiple storeys, linen distribution and catering required strict oversight. Our initial inspection identified that the central linen room and the subterranean staff canteen were critical vulnerability points. By implementing a twelve-visit monthly plan led by technician Amara Mensah, both areas became permanently designated 'always look' inspection points on the building floor plan. Over successive months, documented findings verified ongoing seal integrity, eliminating recurring pest pressures and keeping hotel operations fully compliant with hospitality hygiene standards.

pages.title: Season List
pages.content:
Early slots for the next visit season

The Season List is our priority booking register for commercial property managers across Melbourne. Members receive advance notice of upcoming quarterly inspection windows before our calendar opens publicly.

How does the seasonal inspection dispatch schedule work?

Yanagi Hygiene structures commercial treatments around four discrete seasonal rounds in February, May, August, and November. Because technician calendars fill weeks in advance, we dispatch four concise emails each year—one directly preceding each seasonal cycle. These communications notify facility managers of available inspection hours and seasonal technician routes within their commercial zone. Joining the Season List allows new commercial sites within sixty kilometres of Collingwood to secure preferred arrival windows between 05:30 and 23:00 before general public bookings commence.

What operational benefits does advance seasonal scheduling provide?

Aligning pest management with seasonal building shifts prevents urgent operational disruptions. Joining the list secures your business early access to early morning or late evening inspection times, preventing interference with food service, loading dock deliveries, or tenant access. Desk coordinator Grace Tan manages the seasonal waitlist, ensuring your site is matched with the appropriate specialist—whether Tomás Ferreira for food production or Liam O'Connell for dock facilities. We never transmit promotional material; our notifications are restricted purely to operational booking availability and seasonal preparation guidance.

Join the season list

Four emails a year, one before each visit season. We never share your address.

pages.title: Privacy
pages.content:
How we handle your details

Yanagi Hygiene respects the privacy of facility managers and commercial clients across Melbourne. This policy outlines how we handle site records, contact information, and inspection data.

What information do we collect during inspections and account setup?

We collect operational data required to perform commercial pest control and maintain statutory hygiene records within sixty kilometres of Collingwood. This information includes client names, corporate email addresses, direct telephone numbers, facility street addresses, and building floor plans. During on-site visits, our technicians record specific architectural features, photographs of structural vulnerabilities, gap gauge measurements, and monitor station locations. We also log communication histories, invoice records, and signed findings sheets to support ongoing twelve-month service agreements.

How are commercial site records stored, protected, and retained?

All physical findings sheets and digital inspection reports are archived securely at our Collingwood depot and on encrypted local servers. In accordance with our compliance protocols, site inspection records and treatment histories are retained for the active life of your annual plan plus an additional three years. Data is accessible solely to authorized staff—including Priya Nair, field technicians, and desk coordinator Grace Tan—for the purpose of scheduling visits, generating reports, and addressing compliance audits. We never sell, transfer, or disclose client information to external third parties.

How can you review, correct, or request deletion of stored records?

Facility managers may review or update their stored contact details and site records at any time. Our client desk responds to data access requests within one working day. To request a copy of archived floor plans, update site access instructions, or clarify stored inspection histories, contact our desk at 41 Wellington Street, Collingwood VIC 3066, phone +61 3 9000 0418, or email desk@yanagihygiene.example. Note that statutory compliance logs must be preserved for three years past plan completion to satisfy environmental health auditing requirements.

Our legal commitment is to provide scheduled seasonal visits, inspect hidden building voids, deliver written findings at the end of each hour, email comprehensive reports within two working days, and retain records for the life of the plan plus three years under Victorian commercial jurisdiction.

posts.title: Why the first hour starts at the loading dock
posts.excerpt: A commercial building's most active delivery bay reveals entry paths, hygiene pressures, and structural wear before technicians examine interior workspaces.
posts.content:
When a Yanagi Hygiene technician arrives at a commercial facility for an initial sixty-minute inspection hour, the investigation rarely begins in the front reception or the corporate office suites. Instead, we walk directly to the loading dock alongside the facilities manager. Docks, delivery bays, and receiving ramps represent the primary physical threshold where an enclosed commercial building connects with the outside environment. Every crate, food pallet, cardboard delivery, and waste container moves through this high-traffic zone, creating continuous mechanical wear on doors, guide rails, and perimeter seals while introducing daily pest pressures from transport vehicles across Melbourne.

The first ten minutes of our inspection involve reviewing the site floor plan to observe how goods flow into the facility and where discarded packaging materials sit before collection. Our technicians, including Liam O'Connell who oversees warehouses, distribution centres, and cold storage facilities, carefully inspect the perimeter of roller doors and dock levellers. Equipped with an inspection torch, telescopic mirror, and precision gap gauge, we measure clearances beneath rubber bottom sweeps and vertical brush seals. A gap of nine millimetres beneath an overhead door might appear negligible across a large industrial opening, but to foraging pests, it provides an open, unhindered pathway into the building.

A practical example from our field logbook involves a two thousand four hundred square metre cold-store warehouse in Port Melbourne with four dock doors. During our initial sixty minutes on site, the inspection identified degraded dock perimeter seals where daylight was clearly visible, combined with uncontained plastic pallet-wrap waste accumulated in a rear dispatch corner. While interior freezer racking and storage aisles were orderly, the loading dock perimeter was actively admitting external pests. Rather than recommending widespread chemical applications, our technician mapped the dock seals as urgent structural priorities, establishing a targeted six-visit annual plan focused squarely on physical repair, waste hygiene, and dock monitoring.

Examining the loading bay also exposes the hidden internal service routes that connect with sensitive work areas further inside the building. Cable trays, refrigeration pipe risers, conduit junctions, and plumbing penetrations frequently originate near dock leveler pits before extending upward into ceiling voids and partition walls. When external door seals fail, pests naturally follow these dark utility channels into upper floor kitchenettes, staff amenities, or mechanical plant rooms. By identifying dock seal gaps during the first thirty-five minutes, our technician immediately knows which ceiling tiles and service shafts require closer inspection with the headlamp and mirror.

Between minute thirty-five and fifty, each dock monitor station and structural breach is plotted onto the building floor plan with a unique reference number. By minute sixty, we complete a concise one-page findings sheet on site. The technician and facilities manager review and sign the document together, recording immediate physical adjustments needed and our recommended seasonal visit schedule. By treating the loading dock as a primary structural defence rather than a simple delivery entrance, commercial properties within sixty kilometres of our Collingwood depot can systematically prevent pest harbourage before interior operations are ever compromised.

posts.title: What we teach new technicians in their first week
posts.excerpt: Looking, writing it down and reading a floor plan come before any product.
posts.content:
New technicians spend their first week with a floor plan and a torch, not a canister. Jonas Weber, our entomologist, teaches identification from photographs and from the monitors that come back from the field.

Priya Nair then shows them the findings sheet. If a point is not on the sheet with a number, it did not happen. By Friday every new colleague has walked a site with Hana Yanagi and written one sheet that Priya has read line by line.

posts.title: Bin stores after a long weekend
posts.excerpt: Lids, drains and washdown points tell you most of what you need to know.
posts.content:
A shared bin store is where an office plan is often decided. After a long weekend, lids are left up, drains hold water and bags sit a day longer than planned.

We check the lid seals, lift the drain cover and look at the washdown point. We note what we found, and what your team can change, on a single page before we leave.

posts.title: Rooftop plant rooms in late spring
posts.excerpt: Netting, duct penetrations and roof access are checked every season.
posts.content:
Late spring is when birds look for sheltered ledges, and a plant room has plenty. Our May and August visits include the netting edge, the duct penetrations and the roof hatch.

We photograph nothing that is not on the plan, and we write down what we see rather than what we expect. The next visit date goes on the sheet before we leave.
